description: We are five Systems Engineering bachelors participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. For the Space Mission Design Game, we aim to build an interactive simulator where users make engineering decisions, manage limited resources, and see how mass, energy, budget, fuel, risk, and scientific value affect mission success. We are interested in software, AI, data, design, game development, and space exploration.
summary:
APOGEO is a browser-based 3D game developed by ORIONIX to help young people aged 12 and over learn to design space missions. Available in Spanish and English, it features an orbital reconnaissance mission to the lunar south pole, guided by LYRA, the player's assistant.

We address the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning mission design into interactive decisions: defining a scientific objective, selecting components, balancing resources, testing systems, and operating a probe. We integrate lunar terrain derived from real NASA/LOLA data with simulated observations. A final debrief explains how decisions shaped the results and allows players to return to the hangar to improve their design.

APOGEO aims to make space science and engineering approachable through experimentation. Its importance lies in giving players a space to make mistakes, understand consequences, and try again, encouraging critical thinking and curiosity about space exploration.
details:
APOGEO

APOGEO begins in a 1969 living room, in front of a television. Entering its screen takes the player to an Academy where their first mission awaits. We chose this opening because watching a space adventure from the other side of a screen is also part of our own story.

We are ORIONIX. As children, we watched space missions on television that made us imagine what lay beyond Earth. We learned about our ancestors who observed the stars, the journeys that took humanity to the Moon, and the projects that might one day take us to Mars. Those stories sparked questions of our own: How do you build a rocket? How do you choose its parts? What does it need to travel so far?

We were excited to imagine building one ourselves: choosing its shape, assembling it, and watching it lift off. Over time, we learned that behind that image were engines, instruments, calculations, tests, and many decisions that had to work together. Our curiosity kept leading us to new questions.

When we discovered the Space Mission Design Game challenge, we saw an opportunity to turn those questions into an experience others could explore. The APOGEO Academy began to take shape, with five cadets and LYRA, the flight intelligence accompanying the player. We built a place where choosing a component changes a mission’s possibilities, testing helps uncover problems, and every outcome offers a reason to redesign.

The ORIONIX team at NASA Space Apps Challenge Cajamarca 2026.

The excitement of imagining a rocket became central to what we created. Today, we want to share it with you.

Welcome to APOGEO. The next mission is yours to design.

What did we develop, and how does it work?

When you arrive at the APOGEO Academy, LYRA, your assistant, introduces the mission. You choose its objective: finding a safe site for a future lunar landing or studying illumination for a base. That first choice guides what you will need to build and observe.

LYRA welcomes the player to the APOGEO Academy and guides them through mission preparation.

You then enter the hangar. A crane assembles the components you select: engines, the probe, and instruments. As your rocket takes shape, a dashboard shows how mass, power, budget, data, communications, and available time change.

Spacecraft assembly in APOGEO’s hangar, where each choice changes the mission’s resource requirements.

Every choice has consequences. An instrument can expand your investigation while consuming more power or generating more information than you can transmit. Before launch, you can rehearse your design and test its systems to discover and repair problems.

During flight, you intervene at moments such as stage separation and program the lunar braking maneuver before losing communication behind the Moon. Six reconnaissance passes then let you acquire simulated images over terrain derived from real lunar data, choosing what to keep and send to Earth.

At the end, LYRA helps you review the debrief: what worked, which resources fell short, and how your decisions affected the outcome. You retain your design and return to the hangar with a clearer idea of what you would change.

This is APOGEO: a browser-based 3D game for young people aged 12 and over, available in Spanish and English. Each mission is an opportunity to learn: you choose, build, test your ideas, and discover how to improve them on the next attempt.

What benefits does it offer?

As we developed APOGEO, we examined how to turn each decision into an opportunity to learn. We wanted players building a spacecraft to understand what each component contributes, which resources it needs, and how it affects the whole system.

APOGEO therefore offers a space to experiment with different solutions. You can change a configuration, rehearse it, and compare the results. Limits on power, budget, or communications become situations to resolve, connecting science and engineering concepts to a specific objective.

When something goes wrong, the debrief lets you revisit your decisions. Its explanations help you identify what was missing, what worked, and what you could adjust. Each attempt provides useful information for preparing the next one.

LYRA and the difficulty levels support that journey with guidance and explanations. Beginners can explore with more assistance and take on new responsibilities as they become familiar with the mission.

The benefit we seek lies in that process: the opportunity to test a mission, understand its outcome, and find reasons to improve it.

What impact do we aim to have?

When we imagine APOGEO in other people’s hands, we think of those who share the curiosity we have carried since childhood: watching a launch and wanting to understand how to make it possible.

We want to bring that experience to young people aged 12 and over, giving them a place where questions can become decisions. A place to propose a mission, explore its possibilities, and find an explanation when something does not go as expected.

Through Spanish and English versions and different difficulty levels, we aim to support people with different levels of prior knowledge. We also hope APOGEO can serve as a resource in classrooms and workshops, where a playthrough can spark conversations about science, engineering, and the reasons behind each choice.

To understand that potential better, we want to observe how people experience the game: what sparks their curiosity, where they need help, and what they would change after reviewing their mission. Their experiences can guide future improvements.

We want that first experience to leave people eager to keep asking questions. We hope those drawn by the excitement of building a rocket also develop an interest in understanding how it works.

What tools and technologies did we use?

To bring our ideas to the screen, we built APOGEO with TypeScript, Next.js, and React. The scenes took shape through React Three Fiber and Three.js, allowing us to bring the Academy, hangar, and mission journey together in a browser-based 3D experience.

That world also needed a scientific foundation. We incorporated lunar terrain from the LOLA altimeter, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter resources, and astronomical information from JPL. We adapted publicly available NASA models and recorded their sources to explain where the resources came from.

We used Blender to work on original models, including LYRA and the refuge’s alligators. The team defined their appearance, directed revisions, and approved versions. Codex, connected through MCP, assisted by operating Blender during that process.


For programming, Claude Code assisted us according to the team’s decisions. We used Vitest for automated tests and reviewed the game’s behavior in the browser. Git and GitHub helped us track changes, and Vercel enabled us to publish APOGEO.

This connected design, data, and code. An idea discussed by the team could become a scene, be tested during a playthrough, and return to our working sessions with something concrete to review.

What makes our approach creative?

APOGEO’s creativity lies in connecting an exploration story with engineering decisions that players can make and revisit. References to Chankillo, the 1969 living room, and the Academy link our curiosity about the sky with the possibility of preparing a mission of our own.

LYRA and the five cadets accompany that journey. The hangar makes it possible to see a selection become part of the spacecraft: the crane places components, and the design takes shape as its resources change. We wanted building to feel exciting, with that excitement encouraging players to understand their choices.

We also wanted probe operations to create memorable decisions. Programming a braking maneuver before losing the signal behind the Moon, or choosing which images to transmit, turns mission constraints into situations the player must resolve.

The debrief then brings together the consequences of those choices and allows a return to design. That journey reflects something of our own way of working: imagining a possibility, building it, and discovering how to improve it by testing it.

What factors did we consider during development?

While building APOGEO, we examined how each part contributed to understanding a mission. The scientific objective needed to guide instrument selection, the orbit, and the available resources. We wanted players to recognize those relationships and find an explanation when their design needed changes.

We also considered clarity. We thought about young people encountering these concepts for the first time and how to support them while leaving decisions in their hands. LYRA, difficulty levels, and debrief explanations help adjust that support.

Scientific information was another consideration. We consulted sources for the data and resources used, and sought to distinguish real-world references from approximations and values defined for gameplay. We also paid attention to controls, the readability of conversations, and browser performance.

Finally, we had to decide the scope of the submitted version. We focused the journey on one lunar orbital reconnaissance mission, extending from objective selection through evaluation and redesign. Additional missions remain part of future development.


That scope helped us maintain a shared aim: for players to finish a mission with enough information to explain what happened and decide what they would change when building again.

What we take away from this experience

Looking at the hackathon photographs, we recognize the work behind each APOGEO scene: ideas shared around a table, progress we showed one another, and decisions we gradually turned into parts of the game.

Building it gave us the opportunity to learn together. Physics, programming, design, and storytelling had to come together for a mission to be experienced from beginning to end. In that process, we also learned to listen to proposals, review our work, and adjust our direction.

The curiosity that began in front of a screen took shape as a project we can now share. APOGEO will continue to grow through new missions and what we learn from the people who explore it.

We hope those entering the Academy find some of that same excitement: imagining a spacecraft of their own, taking the step to build it, and wanting to understand what happened after launch.

We are ORIONIX.

Thank you for discovering our story.

Now, the next mission is yours to design.
